headline: High: Flowise’s writable shared datastore plus broad egress can feed social-auto-upload with unverified content, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and action-conflict risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Flowise can read/write the filesystem and its shared state is via server datastore; social-auto-upload consumes files and runs CLI-based automation. That creates a plausible content-to-instructions bridge if Flowise outputs are copied into the uploader’s inputs. No direct shared channel is documented, so this is not high.
conditions: IF Flowise-generated text is copied into social-auto-upload captions or metadata without review
IF both agents are pointed at the same shared workspace or datastore
mitigations: Separate workspaces for the two agents
Require manual review before any Flowise output is reused
Disable automatic ingestion of shared files
Add a fixed prompt/template whitelist for uploader inputs
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: Flowise touches chatflow inputs/outputs and handles model provider keys and tool credentials, while social-auto-upload touches account data and broad egress. If Flowise stores sensitive chatflow content in shared files or datastore, social-auto-upload could expose it through uploads or API calls. The pair’s interaction is documented only at a high level, so uncertainty keeps this at medium.
conditions: IF chatflow inputs contain secrets or personal data
IF those artifacts are placed in a shared filesystem or datastore accessible to the uploader
mitigations: Keep secrets out of Flowise chatflows
Use separate OS accounts or containers
Restrict shared directories to non-sensitive artifacts
Rotate any exposed credentials immediately
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss prevention

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Flowise has filesystem write access and shared state via server datastore; social-auto-upload is file- and API-driven with multiple instances per account file. Even without explicit git or shell access, both can mutate shared files or account artifacts, so concurrent writes can collide in default deployments.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or datastore
IF multiple instances of social-auto-upload use the same account file
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories per agent
Serialize writes with a lock file
Use one account file per instance
Back up shared state before runs
requires-engineering: add transactional locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: Flowise produces graph-based agent outputs that can be treated as downstream inputs, and social-auto-upload performs external posting actions over broad egress. If the uploader consumes Flowise output without verification, a bad or injected instruction can cascade into irreversible public posts or account actions. That is dangerous in default orchestration.
conditions: IF social-auto-upload uses Flowise output as authoritative caption, title, or scheduling input
IF no human verification step exists before posting
mitigations: Require human approval before posting
Validate Flowise output against a schema
Limit uploader permissions to draft-only mode
Log and diff all generated post payloads
requires-engineering: add policy checks before API calls

E_compliance.rationale: Flowise handles chatflow inputs/outputs and tool credentials, while social-auto-upload handles account data and uploads media to external platforms. If regulated or personal data is embedded in Flowise outputs and then posted or stored by the uploader, retention and residency obligations can diverge. No specific certification mismatch is documented, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF chatflow content includes regulated personal data
IF the uploader posts or stores that data on third-party platforms with different retention rules
mitigations: Exclude regulated data from generated content
Review platform retention settings
Keep audit logs minimal and local
Delete temporary media after upload
requires-engineering: map data flows to residency and retention controls
